newsitem.title: FRANCE: Eurocourt rules against Britain in Saunders trial.
newsitem.headline: Eurocourt rules against Britain in Saunders trial.

text.p: The European Court of Human Rights ruled on Tuesday that Britain denied a fair trial to Ernest Saunders, ex-chairman of the Guinness plc drinks group, who was convicted of fraud in 1990.

The judges voted by 16 to four that Britain violated Saunders' rights by forcing him to give statements to government inspectors that were later used as incriminating evidence at his trial. The ruling may force the British government to rein in the powers of its fraud investigators.
It was a fresh defeat in Strasbourg for Britain, already smarting from a string of recent court condemnations including for the killings of three Irish guerrillas in Gibraltar in 1988.

The court ordered Britain to pay Saunders, who was sacked as chairman of Guinness in 1987, 75,000 pounds ($124,500) in legal costs. But it refused him compensation, saying it was unclear whether the violation had affected the outcome of his trial.
The British Department of Trade and Industry said it was disappointed by the ruling of the Strasbourg-based court, an arm of the 40-nation Council of Europe.
"Mr Saunders was convicted by jury after it heard all the evidence," a DTI spokeswoman said.

Saunders, now 61, was convicted in 1990 on 12 counts including false accounting and theft for inflating Guinness' share price to help its 1986 takeover of whisky group Distillers Plc prevail against rival bidder Argyll Plc.
A British Crown Court sentenced him to five years in jail in 1990 but his term was halved in 1991 after doctors found he was suffering from an Alzheimer-type disease. He is now free.

The court agreed with Saunders that evidence obtained from him by DTI inspectors, who can legally oblige suspects to reply to questions or face fines or up to two years in jail, was later used against him in court despite his objections.

"The court stressed that the right not to incriminate oneself, like the right to silence, was a generally-recognised international standard which lay at the heart of the notion of a fair procedure," a Council of Europe statement said.
In refusing compensation, "it could not speculate...whether the outcome of the trial would have been any different had use not been made of the statements by the prosecution".
The judges overwhelmingly followed a 1994 opinion of the European Commission of Human Rights, which vets cases for the court.
British government lawyers argued that a right to silence cannot be absolute, especially for corporate bosses meant to be fully accountable to shareholders.
Tuesday's ruling could lead to actions by the other members of the "Guinness Four" convicted with Saunders -- businessmen Gerald Ronson and Jack Lyons, and financier Tony Parnes.

It seemed bound to fuel long-running controversy in Britain over the right of European courts in Strasbourg and Luxembourg to overrule British justice in the name of European treaties and conventions.
The commission angered Britain in September by agreeing to take up the case of a 12-year-old boy seeking to overturn British laws allowing his parents to spank him.

Earlier this year, the Strasbourg court condemned Britain's system for jailing minors. Most controversially, last year the court condemned Britain for the killings of three unarmed Irish Republican Army guerrillas in Gibraltar in 1988.
